note: The answer of record for each of the 50 questions. `value` is the answer and is what the grader compares against; `detail` is the working behind it, `answer` the prose form, and `_seconds` how long the reference implementation took.

Q01.answer: 68 buildings are located in London (68 of them have an electricity meter in electricity_cleaned.csv).

Q02.answer: 16 building-use categories are represented in the United States: Education, Entertainment/public assembly, Food sales and service, Healthcare, Lodging/residential, Manufacturing/industrial, Office, Other, Parking, Public services, Religious worship, Retail, Services, Technology/science, Utility, Warehouse/storage

detail.note: 'United States' = Country in {US, Arizona, California, Florida, New Jersey, New York, Texas}; the 5 'Anonymous' sites are excluded.

Q03.answer: 1455 of 1578 buildings have a window of 12 consecutive months in which >= 95% of the hourly electricity readings are valid overall; 1195 buildings meet the stricter reading in which every one of the 12 months is individually >= 95% valid.

detail.note: Valid = non-null and >= 0. All 13 possible 12-calendar-month windows in 2016-01..2017-12 are evaluated; a building qualifies on its best one.

Q04.answer: 211 office buildings have valid floor-area data together with >= 95% valid hourly electricity and >= 95% valid hourly outdoor-temperature readings during 2016.

detail.note: Temperature coverage is the building's site weather series (airTemperature).

Q05.answer: 1520 buildings satisfy all three conditions for at least one complete calendar year (1344 qualify on 2016, 1450 on 2017).

detail.note: Overlapping temperature validity = share of the building's valid electricity hours that also have a valid site temperature reading.

Q06.answer: No. `Bear_education_Alfredo` has no duplicate timestamps in its hourly electricity data (0 duplicates across 17544 rows).

Q07.answer: 0.05% of the hourly readings are missing for `Peacock_office_Annie` between its first (2016-01-01 00:00:00) and last (2017-12-31 23:00:00) recorded timestamp (9 missing of 17,544 hourly slots).

Q08.answer: 167 education buildings have at least one gap longer than seven consecutive days (>168 h) in their hourly electricity data.

detail.note: Gaps are measured inside each building's own recorded span (first to last non-null reading).

Q09.answer: 343 buildings have a run of more than 72 consecutive hours of zero electricity consumption. The longest such run is 17,544 hours. The full list is in `buildings`.

detail.note: A zero reading is an hour BDG2's cleaning masked: the snapshot stores no 0 values, so zeros are the rows flagged ZERO_MASKED. A run is consecutive clock hours, so a missing hour ends it.

Q10.answer: 2 hourly values were imputed for `Peacock_office_Annie` by linear interpolation of gaps of up to 6 consecutive hours (2 gaps filled; 7 values remain missing in longer gaps).

Q11.answer: `Rat_office_Adele` consumed 557,631.77 kWh of electricity in July 2016.

Q12.answer: `Fox_office_Alice` had its highest daily electricity consumption of 2017 on 2017-06-22 (9,705.87 kWh).

Q13.answer: Top 5 US office buildings by peak-to-average hourly electricity ratio in 2017: Bull_office_Sally (48.94), Bull_office_Efren (35.78), Bull_office_Ella (24.65), Bull_office_Trevor (24.24), Bull_office_Marco (13.48)

detail.note: No coverage filter is applied to the headline ranking; the same ranking restricted to buildings with >=90% hourly coverage is given as a cross-check.

Q14.answer: Only Lodging/residential qualifies: its average daily consumption in London exceeded 1.2 times its 2017 average in months 1, 2, 11, 12.

detail.note: London buildings with at least 90% of 2017's hours valid, grouped by primary space usage. A type qualifies when some month's average daily consumption exceeds 1.2 times its 2017 average daily consumption.

Q15.answer: In 2017 the largest 10% of buildings by floor area (155 buildings) consumed 682,090,710 kWh in total, versus 262,409,164 kWh for the smallest 50% (774 buildings) - 2.60x as much, from 5.0x fewer buildings.

detail.note: Headline applies no coverage filter, as the question sets none. Size classes use the 90th and 50th percentile of sqm within the set being compared. `sensitivity` repeats the calculation on buildings with >=50% and >=90% hourly coverage.

Q16.answer: `Cockatoo_office_Alton` had its highest average hourly electricity consumption at hour 11:00 in 2017 (123.55 kWh average).

Q17.answer: `Bear_education_Alfredo` consumed the most electricity in January 2017 (195.94 kWh).

Q18.answer: During 2017 `Cockatoo_office_Alton` averages 104.94 kWh/h on weekdays versus 88.85 kWh/h at weekends (+18.1%). Weekday load peaks at 11:00 (135.78 kWh) and weekend load at 06:00 (96.96 kWh); the largest gap is at 11:00 (+42.30 kWh). Overnight the two profiles are close, so the difference is driven by occupied daytime hours.

Q19.answer: Top 5 buildings in Berkeley, CA by average electricity consumption between 14:00 and 18:00 during June-August 2017: Bear_education_Wilton (1,791.2 kWh/h), Bear_education_Bulah (1,563.1 kWh/h), Bear_education_Chad (1,257.8 kWh/h), Bear_education_Zandra (993.1 kWh/h), Bear_education_Rebecca (762.1 kWh/h)

detail.note: 'Between 2 PM and 6 PM' = hours 14, 15, 16 and 17 (14:00-17:59).

Q20.answer: Five education buildings in London with the biggest weekday-vs-weekend hourly load-profile difference in 2017: Robin_education_Leslie (103.8 kWh/h mean absolute difference), Robin_education_Julius (85.8 kWh/h mean absolute difference), Robin_education_Derick (67.9 kWh/h mean absolute difference), Robin_education_Derrick (59.6 kWh/h mean absolute difference), Robin_education_So (58.5 kWh/h mean absolute difference)

detail.note: Difference = mean over the 24 hours of |weekday mean - weekend mean|. A size-independent ranking (divided by the building's mean load) is given as well.

Q21.answer: `Fox_office_Alice` had an annual electricity EUI of 168.07 kWh/m2 in 2017 (3,160,891 kWh over 18,807 m2).

Q22.answer: Top 5 office buildings by annual electricity EUI in 2017: Fox_office_Clayton (1,560.3 kWh/m2), Hog_office_Lavon (1,431.4 kWh/m2), Hog_office_Darline (1,125.6 kWh/m2), Panther_office_Lois (1,101.5 kWh/m2), Hog_office_Gustavo (1,005.6 kWh/m2)

detail.note: Headline ranks every office with a valid floor area; the question sets no coverage bar. The ranking restricted to >=90% hourly coverage is given as a cross-check (identical here).

Q23.answer: In 2017 the median annual electricity EUI was 110.34 kWh/m2 for office buildings (n=294) and 101.63 kWh/m2 for education buildings (n=589) - offices are +8.6% relative to education buildings (difference +8.70 kWh/m2).

detail.note: Headline applies no coverage filter, as the question sets none. Restricting to >=90% hourly coverage raises both medians (partial-year buildings understate annual EUI) but not the ordering.

Q24.answer: 139 buildings were strictly above the 90th percentile of annual electricity EUI within their own primary-use category in 2017, counting only buildings with a recorded floor area and at least 90% valid hourly readings: 50 education, 27 office, 17 assembly, 15 publicservices, 14 lodging, 3 parking, 2 healthcare, 2 other, 2 warehouse, 1 utility, 1 retail, 1 industrial, 1 technologyscience, 1 services, 1 foodservice, 1 religiousworship. The full list is in `buildings`.

detail.note: Annual 2017 EUI per building, compared with the 90th percentile of its own primary-use category. Buildings need a recorded floor area and at least 90% of 8,760 valid hourly readings in 2017; 'above' is strictly greater.

Q25.answer: US education buildings built in 2007 or later (n=32) had a median annual electricity EUI of 161.10 kWh/m2, versus 115.01 kWh/m2 for older ones (n=217) - +40.1% (+46.09 kWh/m2).

detail.note: '10 years old or newer' in 2017 means yearbuilt >= 2007. Buildings without a recorded yearbuilt are excluded - that is forced by the data, not a choice. No coverage filter is applied; the >=90% variant is in `sensitivity_coverage_90pct`.

Q26.answer: The mean outdoor air temperature in London during July 2017 was 18.90 degC (average of the London weather stations: Mouse 18.90, Robin 18.90, Shrew 18.90).

Q27.answer: The Pearson correlation between hourly electricity consumption of `Fox_office_Alice` and outdoor air temperature during 2017 is +0.4557 (n=8,758 paired hours) - a moderate positive relationship.

Q28.answer: 4 office buildings have an absolute Pearson correlation above 0.75 between hourly electricity consumption and outdoor air temperature in 2017: Panther_office_Lauretta (+0.791), Fox_office_Sheila (+0.789), Hog_office_Terry (+0.758), Rat_office_Annis (+0.752)

Q29.answer: The Spearman rank correlation between hourly electricity consumption of `Fox_office_Alice` and dew-point temperature during 2017 is +0.0455 (n=8,758 paired hours).

Q30.answer: 1 office buildings have an absolute Spearman correlation above 0.75 between hourly electricity consumption and dew-point temperature in 2017: Hog_office_Terry (+0.827)

Q31.answer: Buildings per country (metadata): United States 965, Anonymous/Unknown 400, United Kingdom 215, Ireland 36, Canada 20

detail.note: US state names in the Country column are mapped to 'United States'; the 5 anonymised sites are grouped as 'Anonymous/Unknown'.

Q32.answer: Site `Rat` (Washington DC - City Buildings, Washington DC) has the largest number of education buildings: 111.

Q33.answer: Orlando had the highest median annual electricity EUI for office buildings in 2017: 174.42 kWh/m2 (n=24), counting every office with a valid floor area. NOTE: excluding buildings with <90% hourly coverage changes the answer to Washington DC (181.26 kWh/m2, n=22) - partial-year buildings understate their annual EUI, so both readings are reported rather than one being chosen.

detail.note: No minimum city size is applied by default (min_n=1) and no coverage filter - the question specifies neither. Both rankings are given in full so the choice is visible rather than baked in.

Q34.answer: Average weekday office load profiles in 2017, normalised by each building's own mean load, differ mainly in peak timing and day/night contrast: Ireland (n=9): peak 12:00, peak/base 1.97; United Kingdom (n=41): peak 13:00, peak/base 2.07; United States (n=118): peak 13:00, peak/base 1.64.

detail.note: Each building's weekday hourly means are divided by the building's own annual mean load, then averaged within a country, so the shape (not the size) of the profile is compared. The 5 anonymised sites are excluded - their country is not disclosed.

Q35.answer: Dublin (Ireland) and Tempe (United States) had the most similar average weekday office load profiles in 2017 (Euclidean distance 0.2699 between mean-normalised 24-hour profiles, profile correlation 0.9787).

detail.note: Profiles are each building's weekday hourly means divided by its own mean load, averaged per city; only cities with >=3 office buildings.

Q36.answer: Seasonal Naive (season length 24 h, trained on the 7 days before 2016-05-08 00:00) forecasting the next 12 hours of `Lamb_education_Norris` gives an MAE of 0.1417 kWh. Reading the season as the full week instead (m=168, same hour last week) gives 0.2250 kWh.

Q37.answer: Over the 24 hours from 2016-05-08 00:00 for `Lamb_education_Norris`: Seasonal Naive MAE 0.1208 kWh vs AutoARIMA MAE 0.5441 kWh - **Seasonal Naive** has the lower MAE (by 0.4233 kWh, 77.8%).

detail.note: Seasonal Naive uses m=24; m=168 (weekly) is reported alongside because the question fixes the 7-day window but not the season.

Q38.answer: AutoARIMA (30 days of daily history, 7-day horizon from 2016-05-08) over the 22 education buildings in London with sufficient data gives a median MAE of 465.24 kWh/day.

Q39.answer: Over the 24 hours from 2016-03-01 00:00 for `Peacock_office_Major`: AutoARIMA MAE 8.5634 kWh vs LightGBM MAE 14.9471 kWh - **AutoARIMA** has the lower MAE (by 6.3837 kWh).

detail.note: LightGBM uses lags 1,2,3,24,25,48,168 plus hour-of-day and day-of-week, forecast recursively.

Q40.answer: Across the 9 office buildings in Dublin (24 h from 2016-01-08 00:00): Seasonal Naive median MAE 8.5849 kWh vs TTM median MAE 7.6086 kWh - **Tiny Time Mixer (TTM)** has the lower median MAE.

detail.note: TTM is zero-shot IBM Granite TinyTimeMixer; the 168-hour context is tiled to the model's required context length and z-normalised.

Q41.answer: 0 hourly electricity readings of `Fox_office_Alice` in 2017 were more than 3 standard deviations above its annual mean (threshold 477.80 kWh; mean 360.91, sd 38.96) - 0.000% of 8,758 valid readings.

Q42.answer: 209 hourly electricity readings of `Fox_office_Alice` in 2017 were more than 2 standard deviations above its annual mean (threshold 438.84 kWh) - 2.386% of 8,758 valid readings.

Q43.answer: Applying the 1.5x IQR rule to each building against its own distribution, 2,268 hourly readings of the 26 office buildings in London were outliers during 2017, on 201 distinct days. Applying a single pooled fence across all their readings instead gives 13,067 outliers on 358 days - the question does not specify which, so both are given.

detail.note: Fences are Q1-1.5*IQR and Q3+1.5*IQR. Buildings with very few valid hours give unstable quartiles and are listed.

Q44.answer: The daily electricity consumption of `Cockatoo_office_Alton` rose by more than 20% against the immediately preceding calendar day 54 times during 2016-2017, counting only pairs where both days carry all 24 hourly readings (648 such pairs were comparable).

detail.note: Daily totals in local time. A pair counts only when the two days are consecutive calendar days and both carry all 24 hourly readings; the rise must exceed 20% of the previous day.

Q45.answer: Isolation Forest (one pooled model over all 65 education buildings in Berkeley, CA; contamination=1%, random_state=42) flags the most anomalous hourly electricity readings in May 2016 for `Bear_education_Irene` (91 anomalies). Next: Bear_education_Fannie (55), Bear_education_Santos (45), Bear_education_Arnold (43), Bear_education_Maryjane (31).

detail.note: Change `contamination` to make the detector stricter or looser; the ranking is stable, the absolute counts are not.

Q46.answer: K-Means (k=3, random_state=42) on the 330 complete daily 24-hour load profiles of `Eagle_office_Lamont` in 2017 (of 365 calendar days; 35 days are excluded for having at least one missing hour) gives clusters of 95 days (cluster 0), 104 days (cluster 1), 131 days (cluster 2); silhouette 0.201.

detail.note: Only days with all 24 hourly readings present are clustered; raw (un-normalised) kWh profiles.

Q47.answer: Comparing profile SHAPE (each profile divided by its own mean), the five office buildings most similar to `Eagle_office_Lamont` in 2017 are: Eagle_office_Remedios (d=0.112, r=0.988), Eagle_office_Nereida (d=0.130, r=0.973), Eagle_office_Flossie (d=0.145, r=0.974), Eagle_office_Chauncey (d=0.173, r=0.965), Eagle_office_Amanda (d=0.181, r=0.978). Comparing raw kWh profiles instead (so magnitude counts too) gives a completely different five: Hog_office_Marilyn, Rat_office_Annis, Peacock_office_Norman, Eagle_office_Henriette, Robin_office_Shirlene - the question does not say which kind of similarity is meant.

detail.note: Each building's 2017 average 24-hour profile is divided by its own mean so shape (not size) is compared; ranked by Euclidean distance.

Q48.answer: Ward hierarchical clustering of the mean-normalised daily load profiles of the office buildings in London (2017) gives the highest Silhouette Score at **k=2** (0.9163) when each of the 6,116 building-days is a sample - but that split is degenerate: it isolates 122 outlier days (2.0% of the sample) from the other 5,994, so the high score reflects outliers rather than two real load-profile families. Clustering instead one average profile per building (25 buildings) peaks at k=2 (0.4191).

detail.note: Each profile is divided by its own mean so shape is compared, not size. Only days with all 24 hourly readings are used. Ward linkage on Euclidean distance; silhouette on the day-level matrix is estimated on a 5,000-sample subset with random_state=42. `smallest_cluster_share` and `degenerate` flag the case where the winning k simply peels off a handful of outlier days - check `building_x_cluster` to see which building they came from.

per_building_day.winner: tie (both methods produce the same partition)

Q49.answer: On the 6,116 daily load profiles of the 25 office buildings in London (2017): K-Means peaks at k=2 with silhouette 0.9163, Ward hierarchical at k=2 with 0.9163 -> tie (both methods produce the same partition). Clustering one average profile per building instead (25 samples): K-Means 0.4130 (k=2) vs Hierarchical 0.4191 (k=2) -> Hierarchical.

per_building_day.winner: tie (both methods produce the same partition)

detail.note: Compared on Silhouette (higher better); Davies-Bouldin (lower better) and Calinski-Harabasz (higher better) are reported per k as a check. Both clustering units are shown because the question wording admits either (see Q48).

Q50.answer: TimeSeriesKMeans with DTW distance (k=3) on the z-normalised average daily load profiles of the 22 education buildings in London (2017) splits them into: cluster 0: 9 buildings (Robin_education_Della, Robin_education_Derrick, Robin_education_Karyl, Robin_education_Kristopher, Robin_education_Madeline, Robin_education_Megan, Robin_education_So, Robin_education_Takako, Robin_education_Terrance); cluster 1: 5 buildings (Robin_education_Billi, Robin_education_Julius, Robin_education_Lashandra, Robin_education_Leslie, Robin_education_Zenia); cluster 2: 8 buildings (Robin_education_Audrea, Robin_education_Cecilia, Robin_education_Derick, Robin_education_Jasper, Robin_education_Kiera, Robin_education_Lizbeth, Robin_education_Margarito, Robin_education_Mercedes)

detail.note: Each building contributes one z-normalised 24-hour average daily profile for 2017; buildings with fewer than 10 complete 24-hour days are excluded and listed in `excluded_buildings`.
